setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: In the INTUBE study of intubation in critically ill patients across 29 countries, what was the most common major adverse peri-intubation event?

options.B: Cardiovascular instability

explanation: INTUBE found major adverse peri-intubation events in about 45% of patients, with cardiovascular instability the most common (about 43%), followed by severe hypoxaemia (9%) and cardiac arrest (3%). These events were associated with increased mortality, highlighting the need for haemodynamic preparation.
referenceText: Russotto et al. 2021 (INTUBE) [186]; Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: In the PREOXI trial of critically ill adults undergoing emergency intubation, what was the effect of pre-oxygenation with non-invasive ventilation compared with an oxygen mask?

options.A: Lower incidence of hypoxaemia during intubation
options.B: No difference in hypoxaemia
options.E: Longer time to intubation without benefit

explanation: PREOXI randomised 1301 patients and found that pre-oxygenation with NIV reduced hypoxaemia (SpO2 below 85%) during intubation from 18.5% to 9.1%, without increasing aspiration. DAS guidelines recommend NIV or HFNO for pre-oxygenation in hypoxaemic patients.
referenceText: Gibbs et al. 2024 (PREOXI) [73]; Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: What did the DEVICE trial show when comparing video laryngoscopy with direct laryngoscopy for intubation of critically ill adults in emergency departments and ICUs?

options.B: Lower first-attempt success with video laryngoscopy
options.D: Higher first-attempt success with video laryngoscopy
options.E: Higher rates of oesophageal intubation with video laryngoscopy

explanation: DEVICE randomised 1417 patients and found higher first-attempt intubation success with video laryngoscopy (85.1% vs 70.8%), with no difference in severe complications. Video laryngoscopy is now commonly recommended as a first-line device in critically ill patients.
referenceText: Prekker et al. 2023 (DEVICE) [169]; Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: Which score is designed to predict difficult intubation specifically in ICU patients and includes Mallampati III–IV, obstructive sleep apnoea, reduced cervical mobility, limited mouth opening, coma, severe hypoxaemia and a non-anaesthetist operator?

options.B: MACOCHA score

explanation: The MACOCHA score was developed and validated in ICU patients; a score of 3 or more predicts difficult intubation. It includes patient factors (Mallampati, OSA, cervical mobility, mouth opening), pathology (coma, severe hypoxaemia) and operator experience.
referenceText: Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: During emergency intubation, two laryngoscopy attempts and a supraglottic airway fail, facemask ventilation is impossible and SpO2 is 68%. What is the recommended next step?

options.A: A third laryngoscopy attempt with a different blade by the most senior doctor
options.B: Needle cricothyroidotomy with low-pressure oxygen
options.C: Wake the patient up with sugammadex and wait
options.D: Declare CICO and perform scalpel cricothyroidotomy

explanation: In a CICO situation, DAS guidelines recommend immediate front-of-neck access using the scalpel–bougie–tube technique through the cricothyroid membrane. Further attempts at laryngoscopy waste time; waking the patient is rarely feasible in critical illness.
referenceText: Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: What is the most reliable method to confirm tracheal placement of an endotracheal tube?

options.B: Sustained waveform capnography over several breaths
options.C: Chest radiograph showing the tube tip above the carina

explanation: Waveform capnography with a sustained CO2 trace is recommended for confirming tracheal tube placement; "No trace = wrong place". Auscultation, misting and chest radiography are unreliable; a chest radiograph only assesses tube depth.
referenceText: Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]; Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: In which patient is suxamethonium contraindicated because of the risk of life-threatening hyperkalaemia?

options.A: A patient with Guillain–Barré syndrome immobile for 3 weeks
options.B: A patient with burns sustained 2 hours ago
options.C: A patient with hypokalaemia of 3.2 mmol/L after diuretic therapy

explanation: Suxamethonium causes potassium release, exaggerated in conditions with upregulated extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors: denervation (GBS, spinal cord injury, stroke), burns after about 24–48 hours, prolonged immobilisation, myopathies and rhabdomyolysis. Rocuronium is preferred in these patients.
referenceText: Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]; Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: What dose of rocuronium is recommended for rapid sequence intubation, and what reverses it rapidly?

options.B: 0.6 mg/kg; flumazenil

explanation: Rocuronium 1.0–1.2 mg/kg provides intubating conditions similar to suxamethonium within about 60 seconds. Sugammadex encapsulates rocuronium; 16 mg/kg reverses a high dose immediately. Reversal does not guarantee airway rescue, as the underlying problem may persist.
referenceText: Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: A patient in septic shock requires intubation. Which induction approach is most appropriate?

options.A: No induction agent, only neuromuscular blocker
options.B: Reduced-dose ketamine or etomidate, with a vasopressor ready
options.D: Midazolam 0.3 mg/kg as the sole agent
options.E: Propofol 2.5 mg/kg as a rapid bolus to blunt the pressor response

explanation: Haemodynamically unstable patients need reduced doses of agents with less cardiovascular depression (ketamine or etomidate), fluid optimisation and early vasopressor support. Propofol and thiopentone cause marked vasodilatation and myocardial depression. Paralysis without anaesthesia causes awareness.
referenceText: Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: Which adverse effect is specifically associated with a single dose of etomidate?

options.A: Prolonged neuromuscular blockade from plasma cholinesterase inhibition
options.B: Severe bronchospasm

explanation: Etomidate inhibits 11-beta-hydroxylase, causing adrenal suppression for up to 24–48 hours even after a single dose. Whether this worsens outcomes in sepsis is debated. It has minimal cardiovascular depression and is commonly used in unstable patients.
referenceText: Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]; Annane et al. 2017 (CIRCI guideline) [9]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: Which positioning improves laryngoscopic view and functional residual capacity during intubation of an obese ICU patient?

options.A: Ramped position, ear level with sternal notch, with head-up tilt
options.B: Prone position
options.D: Trendelenburg position to increase venous return before induction

explanation: Ramping aligns airway axes and improves laryngoscopic view in obesity; head-up positioning (around 25–30°) increases FRC and prolongs safe apnoea time. Trendelenburg reduces FRC and increases aspiration risk.
referenceText: Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: How can apnoeic oxygenation be provided during laryngoscopy in a hypoxaemic patient?

options.B: Leaving nasal high-flow oxygen running during the apnoeic period
options.C: Bag-mask ventilation with a closed valve
options.D: Increasing FiO2 on the ventilator before the tube is placed
options.E: Using a non-rebreather mask placed over the face during laryngoscopy

explanation: Oxygen delivered by nasal cannula (standard or high-flow) during apnoea maintains alveolar oxygen through mass flow, extending safe apnoea time if the airway is patent. DAS ICU guidelines recommend nasal oxygen during laryngoscopy, alongside pre-oxygenation.
referenceText: Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: Which set of criteria best indicates readiness for a spontaneous breathing trial?

options.A: Improving cause, P/F ≥150 on PEEP ≤8, stable on minimal vasopressors, and spontaneous effort
options.B: Complete resolution of chest radiograph infiltrates and a normal white cell count for 48 hours
options.E: Deep sedation (RASS −4), noradrenaline 0.5 µg/kg/min and a P/F above 300 on PEEP 5

explanation: Daily screening for readiness includes resolution of the acute illness, adequate oxygenation (PaO2/FiO2 ≥150–200 with PEEP ≤5–8 and FiO2 ≤0.4–0.5), haemodynamic stability, ability to initiate inspiratory effort and appropriate sedation level. Radiographic resolution is not required.
referenceText: Ouellette et al. 2017 (ACCP/ATS liberation guideline) [156]; Boles et al. 2007 (weaning consensus) [20]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: What do the 2017 ACCP/ATS guidelines suggest for the initial spontaneous breathing trial in acutely hospitalised patients ventilated for more than 24 hours?

options.A: SBT with inspiratory pressure augmentation (5–8 cmH2O)
options.B: No SBT at all; extubation based on clinical judgement alone
options.D: A 2-hour T-piece trial in all patients

explanation: The ACCP/ATS guideline suggests that the initial SBT be conducted with inspiratory pressure augmentation (5–8 cmH2O) rather than T-piece or CPAP, as this increases SBT success and may modestly improve extubation success. Subirà et al. found a 30-minute pressure support SBT led to higher extubation success than a 2-hour T-piece trial.
referenceText: Ouellette et al. 2017 (ACCP/ATS liberation guideline) [156]; Subirà et al. 2019 (pressure support vs T-piece SBT) [203]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: During a spontaneous breathing trial, a patient has a respiratory rate of 30/min and tidal volume of 300 mL. What is the rapid shallow breathing index?

options.B: 100 breaths/min/L

explanation: RSBI = respiratory rate / tidal volume in litres = 30 / 0.3 = 100 breaths/min/L. Values below 105 are associated with weaning success, although RSBI has modest predictive accuracy and should not be used alone.
referenceText: Boles et al. 2007 (weaning consensus) [20]; Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: Which finding during a spontaneous breathing trial indicates failure?

options.B: Mild increase in PaCO2 from 40 to 44 mmHg
options.C: Respiratory rate of 22/min with comfortable breathing and a stable heart rate throughout
options.D: Respiratory rate >35/min with diaphoresis, accessory muscle use and SpO2 <90%

explanation: SBT failure criteria include tachypnoea above 35/min, SpO2 below 90%, heart rate above 140/min or sustained 20% change, systolic BP above 180 or below 90 mmHg, agitation, diaphoresis and signs of increased work of breathing. Minor physiological changes are expected.
referenceText: Boles et al. 2007 (weaning consensus) [20]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: A patient requires three failed spontaneous breathing trials over 9 days before successful extubation. How is weaning classified according to the international consensus?

options.B: Difficult weaning

explanation: The 2007 international consensus defines simple weaning as extubation after the first SBT, difficult weaning as up to three SBTs or up to 7 days from the first SBT, and prolonged weaning as more than three SBTs or more than 7 days. Prolonged weaning has higher mortality.
referenceText: Boles et al. 2007 (weaning consensus) [20]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: A patient with ischaemic cardiomyopathy repeatedly fails SBTs with tachypnoea, hypertension and desaturation. BNP rises during the trial. What is the most likely cause and treatment?

options.A: Diaphragm paralysis; treat with phrenic nerve pacing and inspiratory training
options.B: Weaning-induced pulmonary oedema; treat with diuretics and vasodilators

explanation: Transition from positive pressure to spontaneous breathing increases venous return and LV afterload, precipitating pulmonary oedema in patients with cardiac dysfunction. Rising BNP, haemoconcentration and echocardiography support the diagnosis; diuretics, nitrates and treating ischaemia improve weaning.
referenceText: Boles et al. 2007 (weaning consensus) [20]; Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: Which ultrasonographic finding suggests diaphragmatic dysfunction that may predict weaning failure?

options.B: B-lines at the lung bases
options.C: Diaphragmatic excursion <10 mm or thickening fraction below about 20–30%
options.D: Diaphragmatic excursion of 25 mm with a thickening fraction above 40% on both sides

explanation: Diaphragm ultrasound measures excursion (M-mode, normal above 10–14 mm) and thickening fraction during spontaneous breathing. Reduced values suggest ventilator-induced or critical illness-associated diaphragm dysfunction and are associated with weaning failure.
referenceText: Boles et al. 2007 (weaning consensus) [20]; Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: A patient intubated for 8 days after a traumatic intubation has no cuff leak. What do ACCP/ATS guidelines suggest?

options.B: Extubate immediately without any additional therapy
options.C: Systemic corticosteroids at least 4 hours before extubation

explanation: In patients at high risk of post-extubation stridor who fail a cuff leak test, ACCP/ATS suggest giving systemic steroids at least 4 hours before extubation (e.g. methylprednisolone 20 mg every 4 hours). Repeating the test is not required before extubation.
referenceText: Ouellette et al. 2017 (ACCP/ATS liberation guideline) [156]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: Thirty minutes after extubation, a patient develops inspiratory stridor with mild respiratory distress and SpO2 94%. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.B: Non-invasive ventilation as definitive therapy for post-extubation stridor
options.C: Nebulised adrenaline and IV corticosteroids, preparing for reintubation

explanation: Post-extubation laryngeal oedema is treated with nebulised adrenaline, IV steroids, head-up positioning and possibly heliox. Experienced airway personnel and equipment must be ready because worsening stridor may require reintubation with a smaller tube.
referenceText: Ouellette et al. 2017 (ACCP/ATS liberation guideline) [156]; Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: A patient with low risk of extubation failure is extubated after a successful SBT. Which post-extubation support has been shown to reduce reintubation compared with conventional oxygen?

options.B: Prophylactic NIV for 72 hours in all patients

explanation: Hernández and colleagues showed that in low-risk patients, HFNO for 24 hours after extubation reduced reintubation compared with conventional oxygen. In high-risk patients, HFNO was non-inferior to NIV. Prophylactic NIV is recommended for high-risk patients, especially those with hypercapnia.
referenceText: Hernández et al. 2016 (post-extubation HFNC vs NIV) [87]; Ouellette et al. 2017 (ACCP/ATS liberation guideline) [156]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: A patient with COPD and hypercapnia during the SBT is considered high risk for extubation failure. What post-extubation strategy reduced reintubation in the HIGH-WEAN trial?

options.B: Immediate tracheostomy
options.D: HFNO alternating with prophylactic NIV, versus HFNO alone
options.E: HFNO alone for 6 hours, followed by conventional oxygen by nasal cannula

explanation: HIGH-WEAN showed that alternating prophylactic NIV with HFNO reduced reintubation within 7 days compared with HFNO alone (11.8% vs 18.2%), especially in hypercapnic patients. ACCP/ATS recommend prophylactic NIV after extubation in high-risk patients ventilated over 24 hours.
referenceText: Thille et al. 2019 (HIGH-WEAN) [211]; Ouellette et al. 2017 (ACCP/ATS liberation guideline) [156]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: A patient develops established hypoxaemic respiratory failure 18 hours after extubation. What does the ERS/ATS guideline suggest regarding rescue NIV?

options.A: Against routine NIV for established post-extubation failure, as it may delay reintubation
options.B: NIV in all patients regardless of cause
options.D: NIV for at least 48 hours before considering any reintubation, in all patients without exception

explanation: Esteban et al. found that NIV for established post-extubation respiratory failure did not reduce reintubation and increased mortality, likely through delayed reintubation. ERS/ATS recommend against it, while recommending prophylactic NIV in high-risk patients.
referenceText: Rochwerg et al. 2017 (ERS/ATS NIV guideline) [181]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: A patient with a COPD exacerbation has pH 7.28, PaCO2 70 mmHg and respiratory rate 28/min despite optimal medical therapy. He is alert and cooperative. What is the most appropriate respiratory support?

options.A: High-concentration oxygen via a non-rebreather mask
options.B: Immediate intubation

explanation: ERS/ATS strongly recommend bilevel NIV for acute hypercapnic respiratory failure in COPD with pH ≤7.35 and PaCO2 above 45 mmHg. NIV reduces intubation and mortality. Oxygen should be titrated to SpO2 88–92% to avoid worsening hypercapnia.
referenceText: Rochwerg et al. 2017 (ERS/ATS NIV guideline) [181]; GOLD 2025 report [79]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: Which condition is a contraindication to NIV?

options.B: Inability to protect the airway with copious secretions
options.E: Mild drowsiness due to hypercapnia that improves with NIV

explanation: Contraindications include cardiac or respiratory arrest, inability to protect the airway, uncontrolled vomiting or upper GI bleeding, facial trauma, recent upper airway or GI surgery, untreated pneumothorax and haemodynamic instability. Hypercapnic drowsiness may improve with NIV under close observation.
referenceText: Rochwerg et al. 2017 (ERS/ATS NIV guideline) [181]; O'Driscoll et al. 2017 (BTS oxygen guideline) [155]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: What is the role of CPAP or bilevel NIV in acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema?

options.A: Should be avoided in hypertensive patients
options.B: Indicated only if PaCO2 is above 60 mmHg
options.C: Recommended in respiratory distress to reduce intubation, possibly lowering mortality
options.D: Only indicated after intubation has failed
options.E: Contraindicated, because positive pressure increases preload and worsens pulmonary congestion

explanation: ERS/ATS recommend bilevel NIV or CPAP for acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. Positive intrathoracic pressure reduces preload and LV afterload, recruits flooded alveoli and reduces work of breathing. Hypotension is a relative caution.
referenceText: Rochwerg et al. 2017 (ERS/ATS NIV guideline) [181]; McDonagh et al. 2021 (ESC heart failure) [134]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: A patient with hypercapnic COPD is started on NIV with IPAP 12 and EPAP 4 cmH2O. After 1 hour, pH has fallen from 7.29 to 7.26 and PaCO2 has risen. Mask fit is good and there is no air leak. What is the most appropriate change?

options.B: Stop NIV and use high-flow oxygen
options.D: Increase EPAP to 15 cmH2O with IPAP unchanged, to splint the small airways open during expiration
options.E: Increase IPAP progressively (e.g. to 18–20 cmH2O), with a low threshold for intubation

explanation: Inadequate ventilation is corrected by increasing the pressure difference (IPAP − EPAP) to augment tidal volume. If pH does not improve within 1–4 hours of optimised NIV, intubation should be considered. Excessive oxygen worsens hypercapnia; raising EPAP alone reduces the pressure support.
referenceText: Rochwerg et al. 2017 (ERS/ATS NIV guideline) [181]; O'Driscoll et al. 2017 (BTS oxygen guideline) [155]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: An obese patient (BMI 48 kg/m²) presents with somnolence, pH 7.30 and PaCO2 75 mmHg, with no obstructive airway disease. What is the most appropriate initial respiratory support?

options.B: CPAP 3 cmH2O
options.C: High-flow oxygen at FiO2 1.0 to correct the hypoxaemia as rapidly as possible
options.D: Bilevel NIV with relatively high EPAP for upper airway obstruction

explanation: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome with acute hypercapnic failure is treated with bilevel NIV; higher EPAP is often needed to splint the upper airway and counter atelectasis, with IPAP to ensure adequate tidal volume. Excessive oxygen without ventilatory support worsens hypercapnia.
referenceText: Rochwerg et al. 2017 (ERS/ATS NIV guideline) [181]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: What do more recent trials suggest about early NIV in immunocompromised patients with acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure?

options.B: Increased mortality compared with oxygen
options.C: No clear mortality benefit compared with oxygen therapy
options.E: NIV is contraindicated in immunocompromised patients

explanation: Older small trials suggested benefit, leading to a conditional ERS/ATS recommendation for early NIV in immunocompromised patients. Larger trials (e.g. Lemiale et al., 2015) found no difference in mortality compared with oxygen therapy, so the choice should be individualised; HFNO is a common alternative.
referenceText: Rochwerg et al. 2017 (ERS/ATS NIV guideline) [181]; Grasselli et al. 2023 (ESICM ARDS guideline) [81]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: What did the TracMan trial find regarding early (within 4 days) versus late (after 10 days) tracheostomy?

options.A: Late tracheostomy increased ICU length of stay by 2 weeks
options.B: Early tracheostomy increased mortality
options.D: Early tracheostomy reduced ventilator-associated pneumonia and 30-day mortality
options.E: No difference in 30-day mortality; many late-group patients never needed one

explanation: TracMan randomised 909 patients and found no difference in 30-day mortality between early and late tracheostomy. About half of patients in the late group never received a tracheostomy, mostly because they were extubated or died, highlighting the difficulty of predicting prolonged ventilation.
referenceText: Young et al. 2013 (TracMan) [245]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: A patient with a tracheostomy formed 3 days ago develops sudden respiratory distress; a suction catheter cannot be passed through the tube after removing the inner cannula. What is the next step?

options.B: Increase ventilator pressures to overcome the obstruction, then re-attempt suction later
options.C: Deflate the cuff; if no better, remove the tube and oxygenate via face and stoma
options.D: Insert a smaller suction catheter forcefully
options.E: Inject saline and continue ventilation through the tube

explanation: The NTSP algorithm: call for help, apply oxygen to face and stoma, remove speaking valve or inner cannula, and test patency with a suction catheter. If the catheter does not pass, deflate the cuff; if the patient is not improving, remove the tube. Oxygenate via face and stoma, and consider oral intubation; a fresh stoma (under 7 days) is unsuitable for blind reinsertion.
referenceText: McGrath et al. 2012 (tracheostomy/laryngectomy emergencies) [135]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: A patient with a total laryngectomy stops breathing. How should oxygenation be delivered?

options.B: Via the neck stoma, as the upper airway no longer connects to the trachea
options.D: Via a facemask over the mouth and nose, with jaw thrust and an oral airway

explanation: After total laryngectomy, the trachea is permanently brought to the skin as an end stoma and the upper airway is disconnected from the lungs. Oxygenation and ventilation must be delivered via the stoma (paediatric facemask, laryngeal mask over the stoma, or stoma intubation).
referenceText: McGrath et al. 2012 (tracheostomy/laryngectomy emergencies) [135]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: Two weeks after percutaneous tracheostomy, a patient has brisk bright-red bleeding around the tube, preceded by a small "herald" bleed. What is the most important diagnosis to consider?

options.B: Granulation tissue

explanation: Tracheo-innominate fistula usually occurs 1–3 weeks after tracheostomy and often follows a sentinel bleed. Immediate management includes overinflating the cuff to tamponade the bleeding, digital compression through the stoma against the sternum, airway protection below the bleeding and emergency surgery.
referenceText: McGrath et al. 2012 (tracheostomy/laryngectomy emergencies) [135]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: In which ICU patient is awake fibreoptic intubation most appropriate?

options.A: A patient with severe hypoxaemia and agitation
options.B: A cooperative, well-oxygenated patient with an unstable cervical spine and limited mouth opening
options.C: A patient with copious airway bleeding
options.E: A patient with septic shock who needs rapid intubation and has a predicted easy airway on assessment

explanation: Awake fibreoptic intubation preserves spontaneous breathing and airway tone and is the technique of choice for predicted difficult airways in cooperative patients with time available. It is unsuitable in uncooperative, profoundly hypoxaemic or bleeding patients.
referenceText: Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: Which practice is recommended by ACCP/ATS to shorten the duration of mechanical ventilation?

options.A: Protocolised ventilator liberation with sedation-minimising protocols
options.B: Weaning by gradually reducing rate in SIMV mode
options.E: Continuous deep sedation until the underlying cause has completely resolved

explanation: The ACCP/ATS guideline suggests protocols for ventilator liberation and for minimising sedation, and recommends early mobilisation protocols. The ABC trial showed that pairing spontaneous awakening trials with SBTs reduced ventilation duration and mortality. SIMV weaning prolongs ventilation.
referenceText: Ouellette et al. 2017 (ACCP/ATS liberation guideline) [156]; Girard et al. 2008 (ABC trial) [75]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: How is extubation failure most commonly defined in weaning research?

options.A: Any desaturation below 92% within 24 hours of extubation, regardless of the cause or treatment
options.B: Failure of the first SBT
options.E: Reintubation within 48–72 hours (up to 7 days in some definitions) of planned extubation

explanation: Extubation failure is usually defined as reintubation within 48–72 hours after planned extubation (some recent studies use 7 days). It occurs in about 10–20% of patients and is associated with increased mortality, largely related to the cause of failure and delay in reintubation.
referenceText: Boles et al. 2007 (weaning consensus) [20]; Ouellette et al. 2017 (ACCP/ATS liberation guideline) [156]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: Which factor is most strongly associated with unplanned (self-) extubation in ICU?

options.B: Use of a cuffed tube
options.D: Deep sedation with RASS −5 and continuous opioid infusion
options.E: Agitation with light sedation and inadequate safeguards

explanation: Self-extubation is associated with agitation, delirium, inadequate sedation, lack of physical restraints in some settings and low nurse-to-patient ratios. Many self-extubated patients during weaning do not require reintubation, suggesting delayed liberation.
referenceText: Klompas et al. 2022 (SHEA/IDSA/APIC VAP prevention) [115]; Devlin et al. 2018 (SCCM PADIS guideline) [54]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: What is the rationale for using heliox (helium–oxygen mixture) in upper airway obstruction?

options.B: It acts as a bronchodilator by direct smooth-muscle relaxation
options.C: Helium increases oxygen diffusion across the alveolar–capillary membrane
options.E: Its low density reduces turbulent flow resistance, decreasing work of breathing

explanation: Helium is much less dense than nitrogen, reducing resistance where flow is turbulent (upper airway obstruction, large airways). Its utility is limited when high FiO2 is required, as the helium fraction (usually 60–80%) determines benefit.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: Which pre-intubation finding is most strongly associated with peri-intubation cardiovascular collapse?

options.B: Normal blood pressure and heart rate with a low lactate level
options.D: High shock index (heart rate/systolic BP above about 0.9)

explanation: A shock index above 0.8–0.9 before intubation is associated with peri-intubation hypotension and arrest. Preparation includes fluid optimisation when appropriate, a running vasopressor, reduced induction doses and attention to oxygenation.
referenceText: Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]; Russotto et al. 2021 (INTUBE) [186]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: What does the ACCP/ATS guideline suggest about rehabilitation for patients ventilated more than 24 hours?

options.A: Passive movements only in all patients
options.B: Mobilisation only after ICU discharge
options.C: Mobilisation contraindicated while on vasopressors in all cases
options.E: Protocolised rehabilitation directed toward early mobilisation

explanation: ACCP/ATS suggest protocolised rehabilitation directed at early mobilisation in acutely hospitalised adults ventilated for more than 24 hours. Schweickert et al. showed early physical and occupational therapy improved functional independence at discharge and reduced ventilator days and delirium.
referenceText: Ouellette et al. 2017 (ACCP/ATS liberation guideline) [156]; Schweickert et al. 2009 (early mobilisation) [191]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: Which criteria support readiness for tracheostomy decannulation?

options.A: Effective cough, manageable secretions and tolerance of cuff deflation and capping
options.B: Persistent requirement for frequent suctioning every 30 minutes, both day and night
options.E: Ongoing intermittent NIV via the tracheostomy

explanation: Decannulation requires an awake patient able to protect the airway, effective cough, manageable secretions, tolerance of cuff deflation and occlusion (capping or speaking valve) for 24–48 hours, and resolution of the reason for tracheostomy.
referenceText: McGrath et al. 2012 (tracheostomy/laryngectomy emergencies) [135]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: What is current evidence regarding cricoid pressure during rapid sequence intubation in the ICU?

options.A: It may worsen the view and should be released if it impedes intubation or ventilation
options.B: It should be maintained during CICO front-of-neck access to prevent aspiration of gastric contents
options.C: It improves the view in all patients
options.D: It definitively prevents aspiration and is mandatory
options.E: It increases lower oesophageal sphincter tone

explanation: Evidence for cricoid pressure is limited; the IRIS trial found no reduction in aspiration. It can impair laryngoscopic view, mask ventilation and supraglottic airway placement and reduces lower oesophageal sphincter tone. DAS recommends releasing it if it causes difficulty.
referenceText: Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: What is the ERS/ATS recommendation regarding NIV for acute asthma?

options.B: No recommendation could be made because of uncertain evidence
options.C: NIV is strongly recommended for all asthma exacerbations
options.E: NIV is recommended only with heliox

explanation: ERS/ATS made no recommendation on NIV in acute asthma because evidence is very uncertain. It may be trialled cautiously in selected patients in a monitored setting without delaying intubation if deterioration occurs.
referenceText: Rochwerg et al. 2017 (ERS/ATS NIV guideline) [181]; GINA 2024 report [78]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: What did the ABC trial (paired spontaneous awakening and breathing trials) show?

options.B: Higher self-extubation rates, with increased reintubation and higher 1-year mortality
options.D: More ventilator-free days and lower 1-year mortality than SBTs with usual sedation

explanation: The ABC trial found that daily spontaneous awakening trials paired with SBTs increased ventilator-free days, reduced ICU and hospital stay, and lowered 1-year mortality (number needed to treat about 7). Self-extubation was more common, but reintubation rates were similar.
referenceText: Girard et al. 2008 (ABC trial) [75]; Devlin et al. 2018 (SCCM PADIS guideline) [54]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: Which factor contributes most to hypotension immediately after intubation and initiation of positive pressure ventilation?

options.A: Reduced venous return from positive intrathoracic pressure plus vasodilating induction agents
options.B: Increased cardiac contractility
options.C: Increased endogenous catecholamine release causing paradoxical systemic vasodilatation after induction

explanation: Positive pressure ventilation lowers venous return, while induction agents reduce sympathetic tone and cause vasodilatation and myocardial depression. Hypovolaemic and shocked patients are especially susceptible; dynamic hyperinflation adds to the risk.
referenceText: Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: Which is a relative contraindication to percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy at the bedside?

options.B: Mechanical ventilation for more than 10 days with high FiO2
options.D: Unidentifiable midline neck anatomy or an unstable cervical spine

explanation: Relative contraindications include difficult or unidentifiable anatomy (obesity, goitre, previous neck surgery), unstable cervical spine, high PEEP or FiO2, uncorrected coagulopathy and infection at the site. Ultrasound and bronchoscopic guidance improve safety.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Young et al. 2013 (TracMan) [245]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: A patient with a COPD exacerbation receives oxygen at 15 L/min via a non-rebreather mask in the ambulance. On arrival, SpO2 is 99% and PaCO2 has risen to 85 mmHg with pH 7.21. What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.B: Continue high-flow oxygen to maintain SpO2 above 98% during transfer
options.E: Titrate oxygen to SpO2 88–92% with controlled delivery and start NIV

explanation: In patients at risk of hypercapnia, uncontrolled oxygen worsens V/Q mismatch, increases dead space and causes CO2 retention through the Haldane effect. Oxygen should be titrated to 88–92% via Venturi mask; abrupt withdrawal can cause dangerous hypoxaemia. NIV is indicated for respiratory acidosis.
referenceText: O'Driscoll et al. 2017 (BTS oxygen guideline) [155]; GOLD 2025 report [79]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: After a failed intubation attempt in the ICU, what is the role of a second-generation supraglottic airway device?

options.A: A definitive airway for prolonged ventilation in ARDS, including patients with high PEEP needs
options.B: A device to provide high PEEP above 20 cmH2O
options.C: A device that eliminates aspiration risk
options.D: A rescue device to restore oxygenation, ideally with a gastric drain, while planning next steps
options.E: A routine first-line device for all ICU intubations

explanation: When intubation fails, DAS recommends attempting oxygenation with a second-generation supraglottic airway (better seal and gastric drainage), which can serve as a conduit for fibreoptic-guided intubation. If oxygenation fails, the CICO pathway is followed.
referenceText: Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]

setTitle: Airway Management, Non-Invasive Support, Weaning and
stem: Which measure is recommended by the DAS/ICS guideline to improve the safety of tracheal intubation in critically ill adults?

options.A: Allowing unlimited laryngoscopy attempts by the most junior doctor
options.B: Performing intubation without pre-oxygenation in hypoxaemic patients to save valuable time
options.C: A pre-intubation checklist with a shared, verbalised plan including backup options
options.D: Waiting for the patient to arrest before intubating

explanation: DAS/ICS guidance emphasises preparation: a checklist, clear team roles, pre-oxygenation, haemodynamic optimisation, a verbalised plan A–D, limited attempts (no more than three, plus one by a more experienced operator) and mandatory capnography. Checklists reduce omissions and complications.
referenceText: Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]
